topic.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves; frequency, wavelength, amplitude and v = f λ
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Waves open P2 in most series. Summer 2025 Higher Q5 was worth 13 marks across the ultrasound threshold [1], a v = f λ calculation with kilohertz [4], particle motion [3], amplitude and wavelength read from a waveform [2], and a frequency from waves counted per minute [3]. Summer 2024 Higher Q5 spent 2 marks on reading the graph, 3 on particle motion and 3 on the wave equation; Summer 2023 Foundation Q2 put the two families in a table and then asked for a speed.
mustMemorise: A wave moves energy from place to place by making the medium vibrate; the medium itself stays where it is
Transverse: the particles vibrate across the line the wave moves along — water waves and electromagnetic waves
Longitudinal: the particles vibrate along the direction of travel — sound and ultrasound, with compressions and rarefactions
Amplitude: the maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position
Wavelength: one complete wave, crest to crest or compression to compression, in metres
Frequency: the number of complete waves passing a point each second, in hertz
v = f λ (m/s, Hz, m) and f = 1 ÷ T (Hz, s), neither of them printed in the paper
notOnThisSpec: The Doppler effect as an equation (red shift appears only as evidence for the Big Bang in §2.5)
Deriving v = f λ, or the wave equation in the form c = f λ with a named constant
Sound intensity, the decibel scale and the structure of the ear

note.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves; frequency, wavelength, amplitude and v = f λ
note.subject: science

mustKnow: v = f λ: wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m)
f = 1 ÷ T: frequency (Hz) = 1 ÷ time for one complete wave (s)
Transverse = vibration across the direction of travel; longitudinal = vibration along it
Amplitude is measured from the rest position, not from trough to crest

mustBeAbleTo: Say what a wave transfers, and what it does not transfer
Distinguish transverse from longitudinal by the motion of the particles, using the word vibrate or oscillate
Give the specification's examples: water waves and electromagnetic waves transverse; sound and ultrasound longitudinal
Name compressions and rarefactions on a longitudinal wave
Read the amplitude from a wave graph, measured from the rest position
Read the wavelength from a displacement-distance graph and the frequency from a displacement-time graph
Write v = f λ from memory before substituting, and rearrange it for a wavelength or a frequency
Convert cm to m, waves per minute to hertz and kilo- prefixes or powers of ten before substituting
Give the unit with every answer, because it usually carries its own mark
sheet.howExamined: P2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed, no formula sheet. Waves normally open the paper. A typical question sorts examples into the two families [1] each, describes particle motion [3] (vibrate [1], at right angles [1], to the direction of travel [1], the last dependent on the second), reads the amplitude and wavelength off a waveform [1] each, then calculates with v = f λ for [3] or [4] as equation, substitution, answer, unit. Higher Tier versions use kilohertz and standard form, displacement-time graphs and waves counted per minute.
traps: Sound or ultrasound written in the transverse column (Summer 2024 P2 F Q1)
The word travel or move where the scheme wants vibrate or oscillate (Summer 2025 P2 F Q1; Summer 2023 P2 F Q2; Summer 2024 P2 H Q5)
Amplitude taken as the full crest-to-trough distance (Summer 2024 P2 H Q5)
The time for one wave handed in as the frequency: for waves counted per minute the period and the frequency were confused (Summer 2025 P2 H Q5)
A prefix left unconverted inside v = f λ, kilohertz or centimetres (Summer 2025 P2 H Q5)
Minutes left unconverted in a P2 calculation (Summer 2025 P2 H Q3, a power calculation; the same slip spoils waves counted per minute)
Powers of ten mistyped when the frequency is in standard form (Summer 2023 P2 H Q5)
A wrong unit on the answer line, where the unit carries its own mark (Summer 2024 P2 F Q1)
Believing only one of the two graphs can show the amplitude (Summer 2023 P2 H Q7)
Confusing ultrasound with ultraviolet: ultrasound is sound, so longitudinal; ultraviolet is electromagnetic, so transverse (Summer 2023 P2 F Q2; Summer 2025 P2 F Q2)

workedExamples.stem:
A loudspeaker produces a note of frequency 440 Hz. In the air of the room the wavelength of the note is 75 cm.
Calculate the speed of sound in the air of the room. [4]

steps.decision: Write the equation before a single number goes down. P2 papers print no equations, and the equation line is normally a mark of its own.
Convert to the unit the equation expects. Metres per second comes out only if the wavelength goes in as metres.

options: Because v = f λ gives m/s only when λ is in metres
Because centimetres are too small to use in physics
Because the frequency is already in hertz
whyMenu.explain: The unit of the answer is built out of the units of the numbers you put in. Hertz times metres gives metres per second; hertz times centimetres gives centimetres per second.

steps.decision: Substitute, keeping the equation's own order so the marker can follow it.
Write the unit on the answer line: it carries its own mark. A check: sound in air is about 330 m/s, so the answer is believable.

twin.stem:
A wave on a stretched spring has a frequency of 8 Hz and a wavelength of 40 cm.
Calculate the speed of the wave in m/s. [4]

workedExamples.stem:
A crest of a sea wave passes a harbour post every 5 s. The distance between one crest and the next is 12 m.
Calculate the speed of the wave. [5]

steps.working: time for one complete wave, T = 5 s
steps.decision: Name what you have been given. The time for one whole wave to pass a point is the period, not the frequency.
The wave equation needs a frequency, so convert the period into one. Write that equation down too.

options: Because 5 s is a period, and v = f λ needs a frequency in hertz
Because 5 s can be written as 5 Hz
Because every wave question starts with f = 1 ÷ T
whyMenu.explain: Seconds and hertz are different quantities. A period of 5 s means a wave every 5 seconds, which is fewer than one wave per second, so the frequency must come out below 1 Hz.

steps.decision: Do the division. The answer is below 1 Hz, exactly as expected for a wave that takes several seconds.
Now the wave equation, written out before the numbers.
Substitute and finish with the unit. A sea wave at a few metres per second is believable.

twin.stem:
One complete wave takes 0.25 s to pass a point.
Calculate the frequency of the wave. [2]

items.stem: Before we start, from P1: which equation gives an average speed?

options.feedback: That one. The wave equation you are about to meet is a cousin of it.
Multiplying gives a bigger number the longer you travel, which cannot be a speed. It is a division.
That is upside down. Distance goes on top.

items.stem: A graph has time along the bottom and displacement up the side. Which axis do you read a time from?

options.feedback: Along the bottom. Two wave graphs in this topic differ only in what that axis shows.
That one shows the displacement. Times are read along the bottom.

items.stem: How many seconds are there in one minute?

options.feedback: 60. A frequency in hertz counts waves per second, so a rate given per minute has to be divided by 60.
Time is not decimal: there are 60 seconds in a minute.
24 is hours in a day. A minute is 60 seconds.

items.stem: In a transverse wave, how do the particles move?
items.skill: Particle motion in a transverse wave

options.text: they vibrate at right angles to the direction the wave travels
options.feedback: Three marking points in one sentence: vibrate, at right angles, and to the way the wave is going.

options.text: they travel at right angles to the direction the wave travels
options.feedback: The angle is right but the verb is not. Examiners look for vibrate or oscillate; travel suggests the particles go somewhere and they do not.

options.text: they vibrate along the direction the wave travels
options.feedback: That is a longitudinal wave. In a transverse wave the vibration is across the direction of travel.

options.text: they are carried along with the wave
options.feedback: A wave transfers energy, not matter. Each particle stays in the same place and vibrates about it.

items.stem: Which of these is a longitudinal wave?
items.skill: Sorting examples into the two families

options.feedback: Ultrasound is sound at a frequency above 20 000 Hz, and sound is longitudinal.
Ultraviolet is electromagnetic, so it is transverse. Examiners have reported these two words being swapped in both directions.
Water waves are transverse: the water bobs up and down across the direction the wave travels.
Microwaves are electromagnetic, so they are transverse. Only sound and ultrasound are longitudinal on this specification.

items.stem: A wave graph shows crests 6 cm above the middle line and troughs 6 cm below it. What is the amplitude?

options.feedback: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position, so it is the height of one crest.
That is the whole distance from trough to crest. Halve it. Summer 2024 examiners named this slip on a P2 Higher graph.
That halves the amplitude instead of halving the peak-to-peak height. Read straight from the middle line to a crest.

options.text: you cannot tell without the wavelength
options.feedback: Amplitude and wavelength are independent: one is read up the displacement axis, the other along the horizontal axis.

items.stem: One complete wave passes a post every 4 s. What is the frequency?

options.feedback: f = 1 ÷ T = 1 ÷ 4. Fewer than one wave a second gives a frequency below 1 Hz.
That is the period with a different unit stuck on it. Summer 2025 examiners recorded a period of two seconds written as two hertz.
That uses half a cycle as the whole period. One complete wave takes 4 s, so f = 1 ÷ 4.
A power of ten has slipped. 1 ÷ 4 is 0.25, and no conversion is needed because the period is already in seconds.

items.stem: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 40 cm. What is its speed in m/s?
items.skill: The wave equation with a conversion

options.feedback: 40 cm is 0.4 m, and 5 × 0.4 = 2 m/s. The conversion comes before the substitution.
The centimetres were left as centimetres. 5 × 40 gives 200 cm/s, which is 2 m/s.
That divides the wavelength by the frequency. In v = f λ the two are multiplied.
That divides the frequency by the wavelength. Multiply instead: v = f λ.

items.stem: Which quantity can be read from a displacement-time graph but not from a displacement-distance graph?
items.skill: Telling the two wave graphs apart

options.feedback: A period is a time, so only the graph with time along the bottom can show it.
Both graphs show the amplitude, because both have displacement up the side. Summer 2023 examiners reported candidates unaware of this.
The other way round: a wavelength is a distance, so it is read from the displacement-distance graph.
Neither graph shows the speed directly. You calculate it from v = f λ once you have two of the quantities.

context.setting: A quick sort of four familiar waves into the two families

parts.stem: State whether a sound wave travelling through air is transverse or longitudinal.

scheme.examinerNote: One answer only: a correct word written beside a wrong one scores nothing.

hints: Think about which way the air particles move compared with the way the sound goes.
parts.workedSolution: Longitudinal. The air particles vibrate backwards and forwards along the same line as the sound travels.

commonErrors.feedback: Sound is longitudinal. Summer 2024 examiners saw sound and ultrasound put in the transverse column of the table. Transverse means the particles vibrate across the direction of travel, and air particles do not do that.

parts.stem: State whether a water wave is transverse or longitudinal.
hints: A duck on a pond bobs up and down while the wave moves across the pond.
parts.workedSolution: Transverse. The water moves up and down while the wave travels forwards.

parts.stem: State whether ultrasound is transverse or longitudinal.

scheme.examinerNote: Ultrasound is sound, so it belongs in the same column as sound.

hints: Ultrasound is sound. Whatever you wrote for sound belongs here too.
parts.workedSolution: Longitudinal. Ultrasound is simply sound at a frequency too high to hear, so it behaves in the same way.

commonErrors.feedback: Ultrasound is sound, so it is longitudinal. Examiners have twice reported ultrasound placed in the transverse column, and once reported it confused with ultraviolet, which is a different thing altogether.

parts.stem: Which one of these is a transverse wave?

options.feedback: Radio waves are electromagnetic, and every electromagnetic wave is transverse.
Sound is longitudinal: the air is squashed and stretched along the direction the sound travels.
Ultrasound is sound, so it is longitudinal wherever it travels.

options.text: a sound wave in a steel rail
options.feedback: Changing the material does not change the family. Sound stays longitudinal.

scheme.for: a radio wave (or any electromagnetic wave)

hints: The two transverse families on this specification are water waves and electromagnetic waves.
parts.workedSolution: A radio wave. Radio waves are part of the electromagnetic spectrum, and all electromagnetic waves are transverse.

context.setting: A ribbon tied to a rope that is being shaken

figures.alt: A long rope carrying a transverse wave, with a ribbon tied to it and an arrow pointing the way the wave moves along the rope.

parts.stem:
A ribbon is tied to a long rope. A transverse wave is sent along the rope.
Describe how the ribbon moves as the wave passes it.

accepted: the ribbon vibrates at right angles to the wave's direction of travel
it oscillates perpendicular to the direction the wave travels

any: direction in which the wave travels

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 examiners named the word travel as the most common error here; the mark is for vibrate or oscillate.

scheme.for: at right angles / perpendicular / at 90 degrees
to the direction the wave travels

hints: Three separate ideas: what the ribbon does, at what angle, and to what.
The ribbon never moves along the rope with the wave.
parts.workedSolution: The ribbon vibrates (oscillates) up and down. It does this at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels, and it stays in the same place along the rope: only the energy moves along.

commonErrors.feedback: The first marking point is for the word vibrate or oscillate. Summer 2025 examiners recorded travel as the most common word written here, and it does not earn the mark because it suggests the ribbon goes along the rope.

pattern.regex: \b(ribbon|particle|it)\b[^;\n]{0,20}\b(moves?|moving|travels?|travelling|goes|carried|pushed)\b[^;\n]{0,14}(along the rope|with the wave|down the rope|along with)

commonErrors.feedback: A wave carries energy, not matter. The ribbon stays at the same point along the rope; write about what it does at that point instead.

context.setting: A skipping rope shaken at a steady rate in a school hall

parts.stem:
A skipping rope is shaken so that it makes 12 complete waves every second. The distance from one crest to the next crest is 25 cm.
Calculate the speed of the wave along the rope in m/s.
Show your working out.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation line is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.
The unit is part of this mark.

hints: 12 complete waves every second is the frequency, in hertz.
The equation needs the wavelength in metres, so convert the centimetres first.
parts.workedSolution: The rope makes 12 waves each second, so the frequency f = 12 Hz. Write the equation before any numbers: v = f λ. The wavelength must be in metres, so λ = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 m. Substituting, v = 12 × 0.25 = 3 m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: The 25 was left in centimetres. Divide by 100 first: the equation gives metres per second only when the wavelength is in metres. Convert, then substitute.
That is the frequency divided by the wavelength. In v = f λ the two are multiplied; dividing is how you go the other way, from a speed to a frequency.

parts.stem:
A second wave on the same rope has a wavelength of 0.5 m and travels at the same speed.
Use your answer to part (a) to calculate the frequency of this second wave.

scheme.for: v = f λ rearranged to f = v ÷ λ

hints: Rearrange v = f λ to make f the subject.
A longer wavelength at the same speed means fewer waves each second.
parts.workedSolution: Start from v = f λ and rearrange: f = v ÷ λ. The speed is the 3 m/s found in part (a), so f = 3 ÷ 0.5 = 6 Hz.

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies the speed by the wavelength. Rearranging v = f λ for the frequency divides: f = v ÷ λ. Write the rearranged equation down before substituting.

figures.alt: A gridded graph of displacement in centimetres against distance in metres, ruled every 1 m across and every 2 cm up. The curve peaks 3 squares above the horizontal axis and troughs 3 squares below it, and one complete wave spans 4 squares across.

parts.stem:
The graph shows a ripple travelling along a shallow tank.
Use the graph to find the amplitude of the wave in cm.

scheme.examinerNote: Measured from the middle line to a crest, not from a crest to a trough.

hints: Amplitude is measured from the rest position, which is the line across the middle.
parts.workedSolution: The curve reaches 6 cm above the middle line and 6 cm below it. The amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position, so the amplitude is 6 cm.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the whole height from the trough to the crest. Amplitude is measured from the rest position to one crest, so halve it. Summer 2024 examiners named this exact slip on this exact kind of graph.

parts.stem: Use the graph to find the wavelength of the wave in m.

scheme.examinerNote: One complete wave, crest to crest or trough to trough.

hints: Measure from one crest to the very next crest, along the distance axis.
parts.workedSolution: One complete wave stretches from a crest at one point to the next crest 4 m further along, so the wavelength is 4 m.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the distance from a crest to the next trough, which is only half a wave. A wavelength is one complete wave: crest to crest, or trough to trough.

parts.stem:
The ripple travels at 10 m/s.
Calculate the frequency of the ripple.

scheme.for: v = f λ, rearranged to f = v ÷ λ
scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation line is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

hints: Use the wavelength you found in part (b).
Frequency comes from dividing the speed by the wavelength.
parts.workedSolution: Write v = f λ, then rearrange to f = v ÷ λ. Substituting the speed and the wavelength read from the graph, f = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 Hz.

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies the speed by the wavelength. To get a frequency, divide: f = v ÷ λ. A quick check is that the answer should be smaller than the speed here.

questions.solutionProgram: amplitude = 6 cm (half of 12); wavelength = 4 m; f = v/lam = 10/4 = 2.5

context.setting: A marker buoy rising and falling in a harbour

parts.stem:
A marker buoy rises and falls as waves pass it. One complete wave passes the buoy every 2.5 s.
State the name given to the time for one complete wave to pass a point.
hints: It is the partner of frequency: one is a time, the other a rate.
parts.workedSolution: It is called the period of the wave, and it is measured in seconds.

parts.stem: Calculate the frequency of the waves.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation line is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

hints: Frequency is one divided by the period.
Fewer than one wave each second means a frequency below 1 Hz.
parts.workedSolution: Frequency and period are reciprocals: f = 1 ÷ T. So f = 1 ÷ 2.5 = 0.4 Hz. Because a whole wave takes longer than a second, the frequency has to come out below 1 Hz.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the period again, in seconds. The frequency is 1 ÷ 2.5. Summer 2025 examiners recorded exactly this swap: a period of 2 s written as a frequency of 2 Hz, when it is 0.5 Hz.

context.setting: An ultrasound scanner sending sound into soft tissue

parts.stem:
An ultrasound scanner sends sound of frequency $3 \times 10^{6}$ Hz into soft tissue. Sound travels through the tissue at 1500 m/s.
Calculate the ultrasound's wavelength inside the tissue.
Give your answer in metres.

scheme.for: v = f λ, rearranged to λ = v ÷ f
scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation line is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

scheme.for: the unit m on the answer line

hints: Type the frequency into the calculator using the exponent key rather than counting zeros.
A big frequency divided into a modest speed gives a very small wavelength.
parts.workedSolution: Write the equation first: v = f λ, so λ = v ÷ f. Substituting, λ = 1500 ÷ 3 × 10⁶ = 0.0005 m, which is 5 × 10⁻⁴ m. Summer 2023 examiners reported powers-of-ten errors on exactly this kind of substitution, so use the calculator's exponent key.

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies the speed by the frequency. Rearranging v = f λ for the wavelength divides: λ = v ÷ f. A wavelength of billions of metres should look wrong straight away.
The power of ten has slipped by one: that is a division by 3 × 10⁵. Key the exponent in with the calculator's exponent button rather than typing the zeros.

context.setting: Two one-line definitions of the kind that open a P2 paper

parts.stem:
Complete the sentence.
A wave transfers ______ from one place to another without the material itself travelling.
hints: One word. It is the thing a wave actually carries.
parts.workedSolution: Energy. The particles of the material vibrate about a fixed position; only the energy moves along.

the number of complete waves per second

scheme.for: the number of waves (passing a point) per second
accept: number of complete vibrations per second

hints: It is a counting rate, not a speed.

parts.workedSolution: The frequency is the number of complete waves that pass a point each second. It is measured in hertz, and 1 Hz means one wave per second.

parts.stem:
A slinky spring lying on a bench is pushed and pulled along its own length, so that compressions travel along it.
State the type of wave travelling along the spring.
hints: The spring is pushed along its own length, not shaken sideways.
parts.workedSolution: Longitudinal. The coils vibrate backwards and forwards along the same line as the wave travels, making compressions and rarefactions.

parts.stem:
24 compressions pass a mark on the bench every second, and the distance from one compression to the next is 0.15 m.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation line is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

hints: Compressions passing a point each second is the frequency.
The distance from one compression to the next is one wavelength.
parts.workedSolution: The frequency is 24 Hz and the wavelength is 0.15 m. Write v = f λ, then substitute: v = 24 × 0.15 = 3.6 m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides the frequency by the wavelength. The equation v = f λ multiplies them. Summer 2025 examiners noted candidates forfeiting every mark on a speed calculation by starting from the wrong equation.

parts.stem:
A wave machine sends waves along a leisure pool. The graph shows the surface of the water at one instant.
Use the graph to write down the amplitude of the waves in cm.
hints: Measure from the middle line up to a crest.
parts.workedSolution: The crest is 4 cm above the middle line, so the amplitude is 4 cm.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the full height from a trough to a crest. Halve it: the amplitude is measured from the rest position.

parts.stem: Use the graph to write down the wavelength of the waves in m.
hints: One complete wave along the distance axis.
parts.workedSolution: Successive crests are 3 m apart, so the wavelength is 3 m.

commonErrors.feedback: Crest to trough is half a wave. Read from one crest to the next crest instead.

parts.stem:
The machine makes 30 waves every minute.
Calculate the frequency of the waves in Hz.
hints: Hertz means waves per second, so the minute has to become seconds.
A minute is 60 seconds.
parts.workedSolution: Hertz counts waves per second, so convert first: 30 waves per minute is 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 waves per second, a frequency of 0.5 Hz.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the number of waves in a minute, not in a second. Divide by 60. Summer 2025 examiners reported candidates forfeiting marks on a P2 calculation for leaving minutes unconverted.

parts.stem: Use your answers to parts (b) and (c) to calculate the speed of the waves.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation line is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

hints: Use the frequency in hertz, not the number of waves per minute.
parts.workedSolution: Write v = f λ. The frequency from part (c) is 0.5 Hz and the wavelength from part (b) is 3 m, so v = 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: The frequency used was 30 waves per minute. The equation needs hertz, so use the 0.5 Hz from part (c). A wave pool running at that speed would be unswimmable, which is the sanity check.

parts.stem:
A swimmer floating on a ring says the wave is carrying her towards the far end of the pool.
Explain why this is not correct.

accepted: the wave carries energy, not water: she vibrates up and down about the same place

scheme.for: the wave transfers energy, not matter / she moves up and down about a fixed point
accept: only energy travels along the pool
reject: the water travels with the wave

hints: What does a wave actually carry from one place to another?
parts.workedSolution: A wave transfers energy, not matter. The water (and the swimmer on it) vibrates up and down about the same position while only the energy travels along the pool.

commonErrors.feedback: The water itself does not travel along the pool. It vibrates up and down about a fixed position, and the energy is what moves forward.

questions.solutionProgram: amp = 4 cm; lam = 3 m; f = 30/60 = 0.5 Hz; v = f*lam = 1.5 m/s

parts.stem:
A data logger records the height of a wave buoy. The graph shows its displacement against time.
Use the graph to find the period of the wave.

scheme.examinerNote: One complete up-and-down cycle, crest to crest on the time axis.

hints: Read from one crest to the very next crest along the time axis.
parts.workedSolution: Successive crests are 4 s apart, so one complete wave takes 4 s: the period is 4 s.

commonErrors.feedback: Crest to trough is only half a cycle. The period is a whole cycle: crest to crest.

parts.stem: Calculate the frequency of the wave.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation line is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

hints: Frequency is the reciprocal of the period.
parts.workedSolution: Using f = 1 ÷ T with the period from part (a), f = 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25 Hz.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the period written again with Hz after it. Do the division: 1 ÷ 4. Summer 2025 examiners named this as the most common error on a P2 Higher wave calculation.

parts.stem:
The wavelength of the wave is 7.2 m.
Calculate the speed of the wave.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation line is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

hints: Use the frequency from part (b), not the period.
parts.workedSolution: Write v = f λ, then substitute the frequency from part (b): v = 0.25 × 7.2 = 1.8 m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: The period was used in place of the frequency, which is the same as dividing by the frequency. The equation needs f in hertz: 0.25 Hz.

parts.stem: State one way in which this water wave differs from a sound wave travelling through the air.

accepted: the water wave is transverse but the sound wave is longitudinal

scheme.for: the water wave is transverse, the sound wave is longitudinal
accept: sound needs a medium of particles that vibrate along the direction of travel
scheme.examinerNote: A comparison needs both sides named.

hints: Name the family each one belongs to.
parts.workedSolution: The water wave is transverse: the water vibrates across the line the wave moves along. The sound wave is longitudinal: the air vibrates along that same line, making compressions and rarefactions.

context.setting: A page for a primary school science display about waves

parts.stem:
A student is writing a page about waves for a primary school display.
Describe how a transverse wave differs from a longitudinal wave, giving one example of each, and explain what is meant by wavelength, frequency and amplitude.
Your written communication is marked here as well: answer in full sentences, in a sensible order, using the specification's own scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: in a transverse wave the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction the wave travels
water waves and electromagnetic waves are transverse
in a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate along the direction the wave travels
sound and ultrasound are longitudinal, with compressions and rarefactions
wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next, or one compression to the next, measured in metres
frequency is the number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz
amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Two families, one example each, then three words defined: that is seven points and you only need five for Band A.
Say what vibrates and in which direction each time; that is where the marks sit.
parts.workedSolution: A wave carries energy from one place to another without carrying the material with it. In a transverse wave the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels; water waves and all electromagnetic waves, such as light, are transverse. In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate backwards and forwards along the same line as the wave travels, making compressions where the particles are squashed together and rarefactions where they are pulled apart; sound and ultrasound are longitudinal. The wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next crest, or from one compression to the next compression, and it is measured in metres. The frequency is the number of complete waves that pass a point each second, measured in hertz. The amplitude is the greatest displacement of a particle from its rest position.

commonErrors.feedback: Sound has been put in the transverse family. Summer 2024 examiners recorded sound and ultrasound given as transverse examples. Sound is longitudinal, and a contradicted point is not counted towards the band.

findTheMistake.stem:
Órlaith is asked: 'A wave has a frequency of 15 Hz and a wavelength of 20 cm. Calculate the speed of the wave in m/s. [4]'
Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The equation is right and so is the order of the numbers, but the wavelength went in as 20 centimetres when the answer was asked for in metres per second. Convert first: 20 cm = 0.2 m, so v = 15 × 0.2 = 3 m/s. The unit of the answer is built from the units you substitute.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of four: the equation line stands, because it is correct physics. What goes is the conversion mark and the two that depend on it. A wave on a bench travelling at 300 m/s would be faster than sound, which is the sanity check worth making before you write the answer down.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ciarán is asked: '48 waves pass a harbour wall every minute. Calculate the frequency of the waves. [3]'
His answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 hands in the time for one wave, 1.25 s, as the frequency. Frequency is waves per second: 48 ÷ 60 = 0.8 Hz, which is also 1 ÷ 1.25.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two lines are right: the waves counted per 60 s and the time for one wave. The last step turns a time into a frequency: divide 1 by it, or divide the count by 60.

prompts.prompt: What does a wave transfer from one place to another, and what does it not transfer?
prompts.answer: It transfers energy. It does not transfer matter: the particles vibrate about a fixed position and stay where they are.

prompts.prompt: In a transverse wave, how do the particles move relative to the direction the wave travels?
prompts.answer: They vibrate (oscillate) at right angles to the direction the wave travels.

prompts.prompt: In a longitudinal wave, how do the particles move, and what two regions does this make?
prompts.answer: They vibrate backwards and forwards along the same line as the wave travels, making compressions where the particles are squashed together and rarefactions where they are pulled apart.

prompts.prompt: Give the specification's two examples of transverse waves and its two examples of longitudinal waves.
prompts.answer: Transverse: water waves and electromagnetic waves. Longitudinal: sound and ultrasound.

prompts.prompt: Define the amplitude and the wavelength of a wave.
prompts.answer: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position. Wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next crest, or one compression to the next compression.

prompts.prompt: Write the wave equation and give the unit of each quantity in it.
prompts.answer: v = f λ. Wave speed v in metres per second (m/s), frequency f in hertz (Hz), wavelength λ in metres (m).

prompts.prompt: How do you get a frequency from a period, and what are the units?
prompts.answer: f = 1 ÷ T. The period T is in seconds and the frequency f is in hertz, so a period of 4 s gives a frequency of 0.25 Hz.

prompts.prompt: A wave graph shows crests 6 cm above the middle line. What is the amplitude, and what is the trap?
prompts.answer: The amplitude is 6 cm. The trap is reading the full crest-to-trough height of 12 cm, which is twice the amplitude.

prompts.prompt: What equation links wave speed, frequency and wavelength?
In a longitudinal wave, which way do the particles vibrate?
prompts.answer: Along the direction the wave travels.

prompts.prompt: What is the amplitude of a wave?
prompts.answer: The greatest displacement of a particle from its rest position.

prompts.prompt: What is the frequency of a wave?
prompts.answer: The number of complete waves passing a point each second.

prompts.prompt: What does a wave transfer from one place to another?
prompts.answer: Energy, not matter: the particles vibrate about a fixed position.

prompts.prompt: In a transverse wave, how do the particles move compared with the wave's direction?
prompts.answer: They vibrate at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
